situation:
You and your teammate are the director of compliance and the director of client operations at MERIDIAN VERIFY, an employment background screening firm. The chief executive officer (judge) has asked the two of you to meet and recommend how the company should handle a problem that surfaced eight weeks after its merger with CLEARPATH SCREENING.

Meridian Verify screens applicants for hospitality and retail employers, and Clearpath brought a records-matching system the two firms have not finished combining. During the transition, roughly 1,200 reports were issued from a partly merged database. A review found that some of them attached court records belonging to a different person with a similar name, and several applicants were turned down on those reports.

When the merger was announced, Meridian Verify told clients and applicants in writing that it would recall and reissue any affected report, notify every applicant involved, and take on no new client integrations until that work was finished. The recall is about half complete. Finishing it will occupy the combined screening staff for most of the next quarter.

This week HARBORLIGHT DINING GROUP, a regional restaurant chain, offered Meridian Verify a three-year contract to screen hires through its restaurant management system, which would route thousands of applications to the company automatically. Harborlight wants the integration live before its hiring season opens next month, and its marketing team wants to announce the partnership. If Meridian Verify cannot start now, Harborlight will sign elsewhere.

Taking the contract now would mean moving screening staff off the recall, and applicants who were wrongly rejected would wait months longer to learn why — the opposite of what the company promised them. Declining it would keep that promise but cost the firm the growth the merger was meant to deliver, at a moment when the two staffs are still deciding whether to trust each other.

The chief executive officer (judge) wants your recommendation on whether to accept the Harborlight contract now or hold it until the recall is done, what the company should disclose about the flawed reports and to whom, and what work rules should govern the combined team going forward. The chief executive officer (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the questions, the chief executive officer (judge) will thank you for your work.
